title: When can local unitaries generate a complete orthogonal basis?
authors: Julian Eisfeld; Hermann Kampermann; Nikolai Wyderka
problem: All four Bell states are related by local unitaries, which is what dense coding uses. Is this special, or can every pure state of a given system be completed to an orthonormal basis using local unitaries alone? A system where this holds for all states is called universally locally encodable (ULE). It was known for \(2\times2\), \(4\times4\) and \(8\times8\), conjectured for two qutrits, and known to fail for four or more qubits.
result: Two qutrits are ULE, which settles the conjecture. The paper also proves ULE for \(d\times2\) for all \(d\), for \(d\times3\) for all \(d\ne5\), for any bipartite system with an infinite-dimensional party, and for two harmonic oscillators. For multipartite systems it shows that ULE fails whenever \(\sum_jd_j^2<\prod_jd_j+n\), which is exactly where a parameter count says it should, extending the four-qubit no-go of Pauwels and Gühne. Operationally, a system is ULE if and only if projective measurements are always optimal in a class of tasks that estimate an unknown random local unitary.
significance: Every state in these systems can carry a dense-coding-style encoding by local operations. The equivalence with measurement optimality ties a geometric property of local-unitary orbits to a question about when general measurements beat projective ones.
limitations: The \(5\times3\) case, general \(d\times d\) and three qubits remain open; the general bipartite case is stated as a conjecture backed by numerical searches. That the parameter count also suffices for ULE is unproven. The two-qutrit proof is an existence argument through a topological covering lemma and gives encoders only implicitly, through phases chosen for each state. The authors state that ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol and GPT-6.1 Sol) assisted with the operational equivalence, the link between regularity and the stabilizer, parts of the constructions (including phases on one boundary arc of the two-qutrit construction and parts of the infinite-dimensional one), a counterexample, and some technical proof steps.

description: A pure state \(\ket\psi\) of \(n\) parties is locally encodable if there are \(D=\prod_jd_j\) local unitaries \(V_j=U^{(1)}_j\otimes\cdots\otimes U^{(n)}_j\) with \(\{V_j\ket\psi\}\) an orthonormal basis. Counting gives a heuristic: the \(D-1\) nontrivial encoders have \((D-1)\sum_j(d_j^2-1)\) real parameters and orthogonality imposes \(D(D-1)\) real constraints, so ULE should hold exactly when \[\sum_jd_j^2\ \ge\ \prod_jd_j+n.\] This always holds for two parties, and for equal local dimensions with three or more parties only for three qubits.

The group approach turns a per-state search into one structural check. If an abelian group \(G\) of \(D\) local unitaries has every element except the identity traceless, then for any state that is an equal-weight superposition of the common eigenbasis with arbitrary phases (a maximally coherent state), the orbit \(\{g\ket\psi\}\) is orthonormal. ULE then follows if every state is locally equivalent to such a state; for two parties this means every Schmidt vector must be reachable by choosing the phases.

For two qutrits the group generated by \(X\otimes X\) and \(Z\otimes Z^2\) has the generalised Bell basis as eigenbasis. The Schmidt spectrum is captured by \((\mathrm{Tr}B^2,\mathrm{Tr}B^3)\), with \(B=A^\dagger A\) and \(A\) the coefficient matrix, which ranges over a two-dimensional region with three boundary arcs: one eigenvalue zero, the two largest equal, the two smallest equal. Appendix C writes explicit phase families tracing each arc and glues them at \((1,0,0)\), \((\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)\) and \((\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)\). A covering lemma then fills the interior.

Further constructions extend the picture. A lifting lemma combines encodings of \(d_A\times d_B\) and \(d_A'\times d_B\) (with \(d_A,d_A'\ge d_B\)) into \((d_A+d_A')\times d_B\). Hurwitz–Radon matrices give ULE whenever the Radon number of \(d_A\) is at least \(d_B\), and with care for convergence this extends to \(\infty\times\infty\). On the negative side, when the counting inequality fails the authors construct a one-uniform state with a discrete stabilizer, which by the Pauwels–Gühne argument cannot be encoded; three qutrits and four qubits are examples.

The operational result concerns estimating a Haar-random local unitary \(V\) from one copy of \(V\rho_0V^\dagger\) with an invariant loss. The optimal covariant POVM is the orbit of one rank-one seed \(\ket\eta\bra\eta\); if \(\ket\eta\) is locally encodable, the encoded basis is a projective measurement with the same loss. Conversely, for a non-encodable state and a small trace-distance tolerance, some POVM strictly beats every projective measurement. The open cases are \(5\times3\), general \(d\times d\) (conjectured via the Bell-basis group whenever \(\gcd(d_A,d_B)>1\)) and three qubits.

methods.technique: Traceless abelian groups give orthonormal orbits
methods.explanation: Constructing \(D\) encoders for each state separately is hopeless in general. A group with traceless nonidentity elements makes orthogonality automatic for a whole family of states, leaving only the question of whether that family reaches every local-equivalence class.
math: Let \(\{\ket{\psi_j}\}\) be the common eigenbasis of \(G\), with \(g\ket{\psi_k}=\lambda_k^{(g)}\ket{\psi_k}\), and \(\ket{\psi(\theta)}=D^{-1/2}\sum_je^{i\theta_j}\ket{\psi_j}\). Then \[\langle g_1\psi(\theta)\vert g_2\psi(\theta)\rangle=\frac1D\sum_k\lambda_k^{(g_1^{-1}g_2)}=\frac{\mathrm{Tr}(g_1^{-1}g_2)}{D}=\delta_{g_1,g_2},\] since the phases cancel on the diagonal and the trace vanishes unless \(g_1=g_2\).

Editorial check: for \(d=3\) the nine operators \((X^iZ^j)\otimes(X^iZ^{2j})\) have trace moduli \(9,0,\dots,0\), all nine generalised Bell states are common eigenvectors, and for random phases the Gram matrix of the orbit differs from the identity by at most \(8\times10^{-16}\).
methods.transfer: When a basis must be generated from one vector by a restricted set of operations, look for an abelian group of allowed operations with vanishing characters off the identity; uniform superpositions of its eigenbasis then work for free, as in dense coding and unitary error bases.

methods.technique: Covering the Schmidt region by a boundary loop
methods.explanation: Showing that the phases reach every Schmidt vector would require solving polynomial equations for each target. It is enough to find a continuous loop of phases whose image runs once around the boundary of the region of possible spectra; a topological argument then forces every interior point to be hit.
math: The region \(\mathcal T_3=\{(\sum\lambda_j^2,\sum\lambda_j^3)\}\) over probability vectors is a curved triangle with corners \((1,1)\), \((\tfrac12,\tfrac14)\) and \((\tfrac13,\tfrac19)\). Editorial reading of the covering step: the phase space \(\mathbb R^{3\times3}\) is contractible, so the loop of phases bounds a disc of phases. If the map to \(\mathcal T_3\) sent that disc into \(\mathcal T_3\) minus an interior point, the boundary loop, which winds once around that point, could be contracted in a punctured region, which is impossible.

On the arc where the two smaller eigenvalues are equal, the construction gives \(B\) the repeated eigenvalue \((2\cos\phi_t+1)^2/27\), which decreases from \(\tfrac13\) to 0 as \(\phi_t\) runs from 0 to \(2\pi/3\).

Editorial checks: the angles quoted in Appendix C.5 give Schmidt vectors \((1,0,0)\), \((\tfrac12,\tfrac12,0)\) and \((\tfrac13,\tfrac13,\tfrac13)\) to six digits; on the last arc at \(t=0.2,0.5,0.8\) the two smaller eigenvalues coincide with \((2\cos\phi_t+1)^2/27\); and 60 random Schmidt targets were each reached by optimising the nine phases, with largest squared residual \(9\times10^{-8}\).
methods.transfer: To show that a parametrised family reaches every point of a compact region, it can be easier to trace the boundary once with a contractible family of parameters than to invert the map; the same degree argument applies to reachable spectra, marginals or moment vectors.
